items.text: Kilmar Abrego Garcia left the United States for Spain Tuesday night, ending a 20-month fight over his deportation, the Department of Homeland Security said.
items.detail: Reuters reported that DHS said he "has self-deported" to Spain, while his lawyers said he left "on his terms." The Washington Post, citing two people briefed, said the departure was part of a negotiated agreement between his attorneys and government lawyers; its terms have not been made public. His flight left just after 10 p.m. Eastern from Dulles after a mechanical delay, and officials removed his ankle GPS monitor beforehand. Abrego Garcia, 31, was wrongly sent to a Salvadoran prison in March 2025 despite a court order, and returned in June 2025 after a Supreme Court order that the government facilitate his return. The administration had sought to deport him to African countries; he had asked to go to Costa Rica. Sen. Chris Van Hollen said the deal respects his will and his due process rights.
items.why: The case, which reached the Supreme Court, was a test of how far the government can go in removing immigrants despite a court order.

items.text: A fast-strengthening coastal storm will bring strong wind, heavy rain and coastal flooding to the East Coast Wednesday and Thanksgiving Day, the National Weather Service says.
items.detail: The Weather Prediction Center said low pressure off the Southeast coast will intensify and track north. Coastal flooding is the biggest concern Wednesday and Thursday, from Georgia and the Carolinas to the Northeast, with high tides and onshore winds. Rain of 1 to 4 inches is forecast for the Carolinas and Mid-Atlantic and 1 to 2 inches for southern New England. Gusts of 50 mph or more are likely along the coast, with 45 mph or more inland to the I-95 corridor, and power outages and tree damage are possible. High Wind Warnings cover parts of New Jersey, Maryland's Eastern Shore, Delaware and Pennsylvania. A Slight Risk of excessive rainfall covers the Carolina coast Wednesday and the northern Mid-Atlantic Thursday.
items.why: The storm lands on the busiest travel days of the year, so delays, outages and flooded roads are likely.

items.text: South Africa's Western Cape High Court on Wednesday set aside the Phala Phala panel report that had revived impeachment proceedings against President Cyril Ramaphosa.
items.detail: The court said the independent panel "fundamentally misconstrued its functions" and made errors of law, and declared invalid all proceedings arising from the report, which effectively ends Parliament's impeachment process for now, Daily Maverick reported. Opposition parties including the ATM, EFF and MK party are expected to appeal. The report concerned the theft of $580,000 from Ramaphosa's farm in 2020; the Constitutional Court revived the process in May 2026. Full reasons for the ruling have not been released, and Speaker Thoko Didiza said she would study it.
items.why: The ruling removes, at least until any appeal, the most direct threat to Ramaphosa's presidency.

items.text: South Korea's stock index fell 6.16% Wednesday to 4,697.51, dropping below 5,000 as the AI trade stumbled again, Yonhap reported.
items.detail: Trading was briefly halted when the Korea Exchange triggered a five-minute sell-side sidecar on program buying, which applies when KOSPI 200 futures drop at least 5%. Samsung Electronics lost 9.87% and SK hynix 11.05%. Yonhap tied the drop to Tuesday's U.S. tech selloff, when Nvidia gave back part of its previous-day jump and concerns over new U.S. tariffs weighed on tech shares. The index had rallied the day before.
items.why: A drop this size in one of the world's biggest chip-making markets shows how jumpy investors are about AI stocks and the threat of new tariffs.

items.text: Huawei, the Chinese telecom giant, was convicted Tuesday of deceiving banks about its business in Iran and stealing trade secrets from U.S. companies.
items.detail: A federal jury in Brooklyn found Huawei guilty on 10 of 12 counts, including bank fraud, wire fraud, sanctions violations and conspiring to steal trade secrets and obstruct justice, but acquitted it of racketeering conspiracy. Prosecutors said Huawei misled HSBC, Standard Chartered and BNP Paribas about its Iran dealings and stole technology over two decades, including Cisco router source code. The trial ran more than two months with over 60 prosecution witnesses. Huawei said the convictions lack legal merit and it will take "all necessary legal actions" to defend itself. The case began in 2018 with the arrest in Canada of CFO Meng Wanzhou, whose charges were later dropped under a deferred prosecution deal. Sentencing has not been set.
items.why: It is the biggest U.S. criminal verdict against a Chinese company, landing as Washington and Beijing try to extend a trade truce that expires Jan. 10.

items.text: The Army's Iowa lead azide blast is set for 9 a.m. Central Wednesday, a FEMA alert said, warning some people within 5 miles they may be evacuated.
items.detail: The alert told people 5 to 20 miles from the Middletown plant to stay indoors with windows closed. FEMA said it is helping residents southwest of the site who choose to leave (1-800-621-3362), and the EPA said it will test homes, schools and properties for lead on request; USDA said about 350 farms could be in the plume's path. At a Tuesday news conference, Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said a controlled, mitigated blast is "far preferable" to an accidental one; officials said crews added sand barriers, water and gel blocks, and that snow and a sharp temperature drop forecast for Wednesday make the 68 barrels less stable. The Army's last lead azide detonation this large was in 1977. Gov. Kim Reynolds now supports the plan after talking with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and Telle said the Army will examine every storage site nationwide.
items.why: Lead dust from the blast could settle on homes and farms in southeast Iowa and nearby states; the Army says waiting risks a bigger, uncontrolled explosion.

items.text: Consumer confidence jumped to 103.3 in November, its highest level since January 2025, the Conference Board said Tuesday.
items.detail: The index rose 11.4 points from an upwardly revised 91.9 in October, far above the roughly 92 economists expected. The present-situation index rose 13.7 points to 132.8 and the expectations index 9.9 points to 83.6. The share of people saying jobs are "plentiful" rose to 30.8% and "hard to get" fell to 18.4%. Twelve-month inflation expectations eased for a second month to 5.7%. The board's economist said the gain may reflect "lower uncertainty following the midterm elections"; confidence rose sharply among Democrats and independents and dipped slightly among Republicans. Consumers still voiced frustration with high prices. Survey period: Nov. 1-17.
items.why: Household mood drives spending heading into the holidays, and markets still expect the Fed to raise rates at its Dec. 8-9 meeting.

items.text: China's anti-corruption agency is investigating Shanghai party chief Chen Jining, a member of the ruling Politburo, state news agency Xinhua said Tuesday.
items.detail: Xinhua said Chen is suspected of "severe violations of discipline and laws," a phrase that usually means corruption. Reuters reported he is the fourth member of the Politburo to be investigated since 2025, after He Weidong, Zhang Youxia and Ma Xingrui. Chen, 62, a former Tsinghua University president, environmental protection minister and Beijing mayor, had been seen as a possible contender for higher office. Analysts quoted by Reuters said the announcement was a surprise.
items.why: Chen led China's financial hub and was viewed as a future top leader, so his fall points to further turmoil at the top of Xi Jinping's government.

items.text: New U.S. strikes on Iran may come after the New Year if talks fail, President Trump told Fox News; Iran's top negotiator said Tuesday it will not talk until its conditions are met.
items.detail: In comments to Fox News on Sunday, Trump said he is inclined to order strikes after the new year without a deal, called Iran's negotiators "professional tap dancers" and said Iran is "more aggressive now than before the election." He dared Iran to challenge the U.S. naval blockade of its ports. On Tuesday, Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran's lead negotiator, told parliament Iran will not negotiate with the United States until its "seven conditions" are met, state-affiliated Mehr News Agency reported. Iran has demanded an end to the blockade, sanctions relief and the release of frozen assets before formal talks.
items.why: It sets a rough timeline for a possible return to full-scale war as indirect talks through Qatar stall.

also.text: USSF-266, a classified Space Force mission, launched on a SpaceX Falcon 9 from Vandenberg Space Force Base, California, Tuesday morning.
also.detail: Liftoff was at 8:08 a.m. PT (11:08 a.m. ET) from Space Launch Complex 4E after several schedule slips. The first-stage booster, on its 29th flight, landed on the Of Course I Still Love You droneship in the Pacific. Payload details were not released.
also.why: National-security launches are building out the Space Force's satellite network.

week.text: Jensen Huang was reinstated as Nvidia's CEO and president Monday, effective immediately, less than two weeks after he resigned; the company's shares jumped about 31%.
week.detail: Nvidia's board voted unanimously to bring Huang back, and to his board seat, after meetings in which it said it was satisfied with his "candor and ability to lead." The board said it received input from "senior levels of the United States government" and is confident his return "poses no national security risk." Huang resigned Nov. 12 after reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman U.S. officials suspected of working for Chinese intelligence; board chair Harvey Jones said on the Nov. 17 earnings call that the board did not intend to reinstate him. President Trump called it "the correct and proper decision" on Truth Social and said the attorney general has no evidence Huang broke the law. Colette Kress, interim CEO since Nov. 12, returns to her finance role. Nvidia closed up about 31.5%, its best day since 2000, adding roughly $900 billion in market value.
week.why: The return of the head of the world's most valuable chipmaker, with the government's blessing, reset the AI trade that dragged stocks into a correction last week.

week.text: The Army will blow up nearly five tons of unstable explosive in Iowa on Wednesday morning, it said, after a federal appeals court cleared the plan Monday night.
week.detail: A three-judge 8th Circuit panel denied the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club's emergency request to keep the EPA's permit on hold, saying the groups were unlikely to win and that the degraded lead azide risks "an uncontrolled and unplanned explosion" without the permit's safeguards; the underlying challenge continues. Earlier Monday, President Trump said the detonation of 68 drums at the Middletown plant would wait for the court and be "fully subject" to Gov.-elect Rob Sand agreeing. Sand did not say yes or no, saying the administration "should make this decision" on the information from its own experts and urging it to share that information with the public. Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said every agency involved agreed the Army should proceed with a "carefully controlled detonation" Wednesday morning, and the Army said Gov. Kim Reynolds supports it.
week.why: The blast could spread lead dust over farms and towns in Iowa and Illinois, and the Army says waiting risks a bigger, uncontrolled explosion as temperatures fall.

week.text: Federal death sentences must be carried out faster, and the death penalty sought for murders of children, under a memorandum President Trump signed Monday.
week.detail: The memorandum directs the Attorney General to pursue federal jurisdiction and seek death for first-degree murder of a minor and murders committed during rape, child sexual exploitation, sex trafficking, kidnapping or human trafficking, on top of crimes named in a January 2025 order. It also orders DOJ to prioritize quick resolution of appeals and habeas petitions, oppose "dilatory" litigation and cut administrative delays. Trump paired it with criticism of California Gov. Gavin Newsom for commuting more than 500 death sentences.
week.why: It pushes federal prosecutors to take over some murder cases states would normally handle and to speed executions.
